Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-0-prompt-long-0105", "row_sha256": "1b4b49fac18e7e7fc216221acdfb818d6dbcbb6efddcb33d61f7604e43da3007", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "okay, can you turn this into a clear brief for making a family photo catalogue from the material we have, not an essay about the family. the folder is called Cedar House Scan Set. it has 46 digital scans and, separately, 12 original prints that have not been scanned yet. there are also four pages of handwritten notes from my mother, Ruth Bell, and two envelopes with writing on them. make clear that the catalogue is based only on the scans, prints, notes, and envelope writing supplied for this job. don't imply that anyone has checked the whole family collection or that these are every photo the family owns.

we need a usable catalogue, not a history that fills gaps. for each image, make one entry, and include the scan filename exactly as it appears, or, for one of the 12 prints, a temporary identifier in the form PRINT-01 through PRINT-12. don't rename files. include the people who can be identified from the materials, the visible setting, any date or date range that's actually supported, and a short description of what's happening in the picture. keep the wording plain. the physical prints should be listed too even though there aren't scans for them yet; be clear about that difference and don't describe what can't be seen. if a note clearly refers to a photo, connect them, but don't force a connection just because the note and photo share a first name.

some likely useful details: the scans are a mixture from the Bell and Navarro sides of the family. the filenames include scan_0041.jpg to scan_0086.jpg, though that doesn't tell us when the photos were taken. the handwritten notes mention Ruth, her brother Daniel, and their cousin Eva, and a few of the notes have no date. one envelope is labeled "Lake cabin, July 1978" and the other says "Navarro reunion?" with a question mark. use those exact words if transcribing the envelope labels. don't turn the question mark into a confirmed event. one note says, "Daniel in the blue jacket, maybe at the station." keep the uncertainty in that description; it doesn't prove where the picture was taken. there is also a scan that looks like a school gym, but nobody has identified the people in it yet. don't assign names to them based on resemblance.

please arrange the result so a relative can find things quickly. start with a short scope note, then make a numbered catalogue section with entries in the order the files are supplied; put the prints after the scans in the order of their temporary identifiers. each entry should show the source identifier, people, place or setting, date, and description, in that order. if any of those details are unavailable, write "Not recorded" rather than guessing. dates can be approximate only when the supplied material supports the approximation, and label them as approximate. don't silently treat a filename number as a date. if an entry has a likely but unconfirmed identification, label it "possible" and say what supplied clue supports it. distinguish what is visible in an image from what a note or envelope says.

then add a separate section for the four handwritten pages and two envelope labels, with a transcription of legible wording and the source page or envelope identified. keep original spelling and meaningful punctuation in the transcriptions. where a word genuinely can't be read, mark only that word as [illegible]; don't guess from context. don't correct the writer's wording. a note may be cross-referenced to an image entry when there is a clear link, but the transcription still belongs in the notes section. if the handwriting isn't clear enough to decide whether it refers to someone or somewhere, say so rather than resolving it.

there are family details in these papers, so keep the catalogue respectful and neutral. do not add personal judgments, speculate about relationships, infer sensitive information, or include details that are not relevant to identifying or describing the material. don't write a family biography or make claims about the people beyond what the supplied material supports. the catalogue may mention the Bell and Navarro family labels because they are used in the filenames and notes, but don't assume that a surname alone establishes who is pictured. do not combine two images into one entry even if they seem to show the same event; any possible match can be noted briefly without treating it as certain.

at the end, add a short section called "Review of coverage." assess only whether the requested catalogue elements are present for the supplied 46 scans, 12 prints, four note pages, and two envelopes. if some source material or detail is missing or unreadable, name that limitation and state what it affects. this is a check on the catalogue's coverage, not a claim that the family collection itself is complete. if the supplied material doesn't support a conclusion about a particular item, say that directly. keep that final assessment separate from the entries, and don't add a recommendation or a general family summary.", "output": "Create a clear, practical catalogue of the supplied family photo materials. This is a catalogue, not a family history or biography.

## Scope

Use only the materials supplied for this job: the folder **Cedar House Scan Set**, containing 46 digital scans; 12 original prints, which have not yet been scanned; four pages of handwritten notes from Ruth Bell; and two envelopes with writing on them. Do not imply that these materials represent the whole family collection or every photo the family owns.

The scans are from the Bell and Navarro sides of the family. Filenames include `scan_0041.jpg` to `scan_0086.jpg`, but filename numbers do not establish when a photo was taken. List the prints separately from the scans and make clear that they have not been scanned. Do not describe details that cannot be seen in the supplied material.

## 1. Numbered catalogue

Create one entry for each image. List scans in the order supplied, followed by the 12 prints in temporary-identifier order. Preserve scan filenames exactly; do not rename files. Identify prints as `PRINT-01` through `PRINT-12`.

For each entry, provide the following fields in this order:

1. **Source identifier**
2. **People**
3. **Place or setting**
4. **Date**
5. **Description**

Use plain wording. For unavailable details, write **“Not recorded”** rather than guessing. Include people who can be identified from the supplied materials, the visible setting, any supported date or date range, and a short description of what is happening. Use an approximate date only when the supplied material supports it, and label it as approximate. Do not infer a date from a filename number.

Distinguish visible information from information stated in a note or on an envelope. If a note clearly refers to a photo, cross-reference the two; do not make a connection solely because a note and photo share a first name. For a likely but unconfirmed identification, label it **“possible”** and state the supplied clue supporting it. Do not assign names based on resemblance. Do not combine images that may show the same event; you may briefly note a possible match without presenting it as certain.

The handwritten notes mention Ruth, her brother Daniel, and their cousin Eva; some notes are undated. One reads, **“Daniel in the blue jacket, maybe at the station.”** Preserve the uncertainty: this does not establish where the picture was taken. One scan appears to show a school gym, but nobody has identified the people in it.

## 2. Notes and envelope labels

Add a separate section for the four handwritten pages and the two envelope labels. Identify the source page or envelope and transcribe legible wording, preserving original spelling and meaningful punctuation. If a word genuinely cannot be read, mark only that word as **[illegible]**. Do not guess from context or correct the writer’s wording. If the handwriting does not clearly establish whether it refers to a person or place, say so rather than resolving the uncertainty.

Transcribe the envelope labels exactly: **“Lake cabin, July 1978”** and **“Navarro reunion?”** Keep the question mark; do not present the possible reunion as a confirmed event. A note may be cross-referenced to a catalogue entry when there is a clear link, but its transcription must remain in this section.

## 3. Review of coverage

Finish with a short section titled **“Review of coverage.”** Assess only whether the requested catalogue elements are present for the supplied 46 scans, 12 prints, four note pages, and two envelopes. Identify any missing or unreadable source material or details, and state what each limitation affects. This review concerns coverage of the supplied materials, not completeness of the family’s collection. If the supplied material does not support a conclusion about a particular item, say so directly. Keep this assessment separate from the entries; do not add a recommendation or a general family summary.

Throughout, use a respectful, neutral tone. Do not add personal judgments, speculate about relationships, infer sensitive information, or include details irrelevant to identifying or describing the materials. Do not make claims about people beyond what the supplied material supports. The Bell and Navarro labels may be used where they appear in filenames or notes, but a surname alone does not establish who is pictured."}]
